originalTitle: Melon-gate was a non-issue in Japan. How did it get elevated to a crisis in Australia? | Malcolm Farr
summary: Anthony Albanese’s comments about melons given to him by Japanese prime minister Sanae Takaichi continue to make headlines weeks after they were made
content: The government continues to face an all-out effort, led by parts of the media, to depict Anthony Albanese as the Benny Hill of international diplomacy endangering Australia’s regional standing. There is ongoing anger – or so we’re told – over a crude double entendre from the Australian prime minister made over a month ago that indirectly involved his Japanese counterpart Sanae Takaichi and her gift of two melons during her recent Australian visit. The incident initially produced the kind of sniggering usually found in a schoolyard, and grave demands for public apologies. Now the opposition has now referred the leak of a diplomatic note sent by Japan to Australia to the federal police, prompting housing minister Clare O’Neil to declare the Liberals have “lost the plot”. There has been encouragement for Tokyo to deliver outrage and condemnation, with the issue resurfacing after former Japanese ambassador to Australia Shingo Yamagami criticised the exchange in The Australian on Monday. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email However, the Japanese government has insisted it is more concerned about the condition of its national economy than a crudity pinned to the Australian prime minister. “It was a non-issue in Japan, not even reported by any of the mainstream press,” Shiro Armstrong, professor of economics and director of the Australia-Japan Research Centre at the Australian National University, told the ABC last week. The controversy may be stored away in the minds of Japanese business and political figures for possible future use, but for now it seems to have a limited use. Yet some persistent media coverage of the prime minister’s comments – which were made last month on a podcast that encourages guests to shed any staidness – has elevated the matter to a crisis. “The fact is … here you and I are on our national broadcaster talking about the remarks of the Australian prime minister which implies being vulgar and crude to a female leader …. This is a national embarrassment,” Liberal Ted O’Brien sternly told ABC radio on Tuesday morning. There is a sneaky suspicion O’Brien liked that prominence, even though it was a relatively short element of the broader interview. The finance minister, Katy Gallagher, told ABC on Tuesday morning the melon comments “were not intended to be interpreted the way that our political opponents and some media outlets are reporting”. “I think they’ve been interpreted in a way that he never intended and absolutely rejects,” said the senator. But One Nation’s Barnaby Joyce argued – without supporting detail – that it would damage trade relations with Japan, but focused on Albanese. “He’s trying to be clever. It wasn’t clever for the fourth biggest economy in the world, an absolutely vital strategic partner in our defence,” he said. The tone of the offending podcast played a part in the controversy, possibly exceeding anything Albanese said. The host, comedian Nikki Osborne, led the way as she pressed Albanese with insinuations the melons were smuggled in under Takaichi’s clothing. “I don’t know, ‘I got a couple of melons,’” Albanese replied with a grin while gesturing to his chest. That gesture condemned Albanese, and Osborne swiftly removed any doubt about his depiction. “She brought two? She just came in looking like Pamela Anderson,” she said. The prime minister replied: “She brought two, and they’re beautiful.” It was the second time Osborne had pointed the prime minister into troubling territory, and he had obliged. On the first occasion he implied he would “shag” Kylie Minogue. Joyce perhaps was right when he said Albanese was “trying to be clever”. It is one thing for a prime minister wanting to reach younger voters through non-mainstream media, such as podcasts. However, there is a layer of dignity that comes with the office, and that should not be shed. Albanese refused to apologise for the comments in question time on Tuesday, saying Australia and Japan have “never been closer”. Hopefully he will absorb the lesson of the melons and apply a discipline to future, similar occasions. Meanwhile, there is a country to run. Malcolm Farr worked in the Canberra press gallery from 1991 to 2019, reporting mainly for the Daily Telegraph and news.com.au. He has later contributed to Guardian Australia, Crikey and the ABC
chineseTitle: 瓜门在日本不是问题。它是如何在澳大利亚升级为一场危机的？ |马尔科姆·法尔
chineseSummary: 安东尼·阿尔巴内塞 (Anthony Albanese) 对日本首相高市早苗送给他的瓜的评论在发表几周后继续成为头条新闻
chineseContent: 政府继续面临着由部分媒体主导的全力攻击，将安东尼·阿尔巴内斯描绘成国际外交领域的班尼·希尔，危及澳大利亚的地区地位。人们一直对澳大利亚总理一个多月前的粗鲁双关语感到愤怒——或者说我们是这么听说的，这间接涉及到日本首相高市早苗以及她在最近访问澳大利亚期间赠送的两个瓜。这一事件最初引发了校园里常见的窃笑声，并强烈要求公开道歉。现在，反对党已将日本向澳大利亚发送的外交照会的泄露事件提交给联邦警察，促使住房部长克莱尔·奥尼尔(Clare O’Neil)宣布自由党“失去了阴谋”。日本前驻澳大利亚大使山上真吾周一在《澳大利亚人报》上批评这一言论后，这一问题再次浮出水面，此举鼓励东京表达愤怒和谴责。然而，日本政府坚称，它更关心的是本国经济状况，而不是指责澳大利亚首相的粗暴行为。 “这在日本不是什么问题，甚至没有任何主流媒体报道过，”澳大利亚国立大学经济学教授兼澳大利亚-日本研究中心主任希罗·阿姆斯特朗上周告诉美国广播公司。这场争议可能会储存在日本商界和政界人士的脑海中，以备将来使用，但目前来看，它的用途似乎有限。然而，一些媒体对总理言论的持续报道——上个月在一个播客上发表的鼓励客人摆脱任何拘谨的言论——已经将此事升级为一场危机。
whyItMatters: 这条信息属于全球新闻信号，适合用于观察外部环境、政策变化、地缘风险和市场情绪。
